The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed 518 Antifungals Blastomycosis Blastomycosis (not to be confused with South American blastomycosis, see Paracoccidioidomycosis, below) is an infection caused by the fungus Blastomyces dermatitidis, which is endemic to much of North America. Inhalation of spores results in pulmonary infection which may be fol- lowed in 25 to 40% of patients by dissemination; the skin, skeleton, and genito-urinary system may become infected. While blastomycosis may affect anyone living in an en- demic area, disseminated disease (including CNS involve- ment) is more common in immunocompromised patients. Acute pulmonary infection may be mild and self-limiting in immunocompetent patients, but treatment should be considered in patients presenting with clinical symptoms. All patients with moderate to severe pneumonia or dissem- inated disease, and all immunocompromised patients re- quire treatment.1 In immunocompetent patients, mild to moderate disease is treated with oral itraconazole; the duration of treatment is at least 6 months for pulmonary disease and 12 months for bone disease. Ketoconazole or fluconazole are less effec- tive alternatives (and ketoconazole is more toxic); the role of voriconazole or posaconazole is not clear, although they may be effective.
